fields.claim_quote: So I figured since the problem is a k-Matroid (is this a common term?) there will be a an approximation factor $\frac{1}{k-\epsilon}$ for  any $\epsilon > 0.$
fields.explanation: The selected instance has three length-2 jobs: the middle interval [1,3) has profit 3 and the two compatible outer intervals [0,2),[2,4) have profit 2 each. Profit-greedy uniquely chooses the middle job and earns 3; the outer pair is feasible and earns 4. With k=1 and epsilon=1/2, the claimed lower bound would be 4/(1-1/2)=8, so this instance refutes that guarantee. The selected theorem verifies well-formedness, the length ratio, greedy value and the feasible comparison. No universal worst-case guarantee, exhaustive search total or global optimality study is asserted.
fields.flaw: The greedy algorithm (take the feasible job of biggest profit) on this fixed-start-time job-scheduling problem, where job lengths differ by at most a factor k (max_i |j_i| <= k * min_i |j_i|), achieves approximation factor 1/(k-epsilon) for any epsilon > 0; in particular for k = 1 (all lengths equal) this asserts greedy is (near-)optimal.

fields.witness: Use the three jobs(start,length,deadline,profit)=(0,2,2,2),(1,2,3,3),(2,2,4,2). All lengths are2, so k=1. Profit-greedy first takes the unique maximum-profit middle interval[1,3), excludes both outer intervals, and earns3. The outer intervals[0,2) and[2,4) are compatible and earn4. For epsilon=1/2,3<4/(1-1/2)=8, contradicting the proposed guarantee. The selected theorem certifies this epsilon and feasible comparison.
